1600:
In history, on February 11, 1967, the Workers' General Headquarters issued a notice dissolving the regiments. On the 25th Huang Jinhai lured Geng Jinzhang to No. 31 State Cotton Mill and had him seized. The same day Wang Hongwen arrested Fan Zuodong, a member of the WGHQ Standing Committee, at the Jing'an District Cultural Center. Through spring and summer, Shanghai Diesel Liansi and the Support-Liansi Station called for a “second great upheaval.” In July Xie Fuxi of The East Is Red was beaten to death by Liansi. In the early hours of August 4, after a rally in People's Square, a huge crowd stormed the Liansi building. It was the largest armed clash of the Cultural Revolution in Shanghai. Mao Zedong was in Shanghai at the time and approved of it. In 1968 Wang Hongwen took charge of a Workers' Propaganda Team of 100,000 people. In October he attended the Twelfth Plenum as a nonvoting delegate, where Mao Zedong said in front of everyone, “Let me introduce someone. His name is Wang Hongwen. Stand up and let them have a look.” The same meeting expelled Liu Shaoqi from the Party for good. In 1969 he was elected to the Central Committee at the Ninth Party Congress. After the September 13 Incident in 1971, he helped Xu Shiyou lure Wang Weiguo into a trap at the Jinjiang Hotel and arrest him. In September 1972 he was transferred to Beijing.

In these five years, Shanghai's worker rebels changed from mass organizations into organs of power, and Wang Hongwen changed from a rebel commander into a candidate for successor.

1611: Book of the Later Han: Biography of Liu Penzi
1612: Liu Penzi was a cowherd boy in the Red Eyebrows army at the end of the Western Han. Because he descended from the Han imperial house, the Red Eyebrows chose him by drawing lots and made him emperor. He was a puppet for two years, then surrendered to Liu Xiu, was treated well, and died of old age. In 1973 Mao Zedong had Wang Hongwen read this biography, with Zhu Yongjia of the Shanghai writing group explaining it. Readers took it different ways. Some said it warned him not to be a puppet. Some said it told him a cowherd could become emperor too. Others said it hinted at a way out. No one knows what Mao Zedong himself meant.
1615: A lecturer in the Fudan University history department and head of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee writing group. He helped Yao Wenyuan write “On the Newly Written Historical Play Hai Rui Dismissed from Office” (《评新编历史剧〈海瑞罢官〉》). In 1973 he explained the “Biography of Liu Penzi” to Wang Hongwen. On October 8, 1976, at a meeting of the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, he argued for armed resistance and said they should “make another Paris Commune.” He was later sentenced to 14 years. In old age he made his living annotating and translating classical texts for San Min Book Company in Taiwan. When Zhu Xueqin asked him why he had argued for an uprising in 1976, he said, “They treated me well.”
1618: Held August 24 to 28, 1973. Wang Hongwen gave the report on revising the Party Constitution. The First Plenum of the Tenth Central Committee elected him Vice Chairman of the Central Committee and a member of the Politburo Standing Committee. He was 38, and nominally the third-ranking leader. On the closing day Mao Zedong was unwell and absent, and he asked Wang Hongwen to cast his vote for him. Outsiders widely saw him as the second successor after Lin Biao.
1622: On July 17, 1974, at a Politburo meeting, Mao Zedong criticized Jiang Qing, Wang Hongwen, Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan as a “little faction of four.” In December he told Wang Hongwen, “Don't form a Gang of Four.” After October 1976 the name became the official verdict. Wang Hongwen was the youngest of the four, the most junior, and the only worker.
1625: At the end of 1973, Jiangnan Shipyard finished the 10,000-ton oceangoing freighter Fengqing. The Ministry of Communications thought its main engine had problems and wanted it to sail near-sea routes first. The Shanghai side called this worshipping foreign things. In 1974 the ship came back from a voyage to Romania, and Shanghai publicized it loudly. Li Guotang and Gu Wenguang, sent by the Ministry of Communications, were held in Shanghai and put through struggle sessions. At the Politburo meeting on October 17, Jiang Qing used the affair to press Deng Xiaoping to take a position, and Deng Xiaoping walked out. The next day Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha to complain to Mao Zedong.
1628: On October 18, 1974, without telling the other Politburo members, Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha to report to Mao Zedong. He said Beijing now had a strong smell of the Lushan Conference, aimed at Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping. Mao Zedong said, “If you have objections, raise them face to face. Doing it this way is no good. You must get along well with Comrade Xiaoping. When you go back, talk more with the Premier and Comrade Jianying. Don't gang up with Jiang Qing. Watch out for her.” In December he told Wang Hongwen again, “Don't form a Gang of Four.” This was the turning point of Wang Hongwen's political life.
1631: A big-character poster put up on Beijing Road in Guangzhou in November 1974, titled “On Socialist Democracy and the Legal System” and signed Li Yizhe, a name made from one character each of Li Zhengtian, Chen Yiyang and Wang Xizhe. It ran to more than 26,000 characters. Under the banner of criticizing the “Lin Biao system,” it called for democracy and rule of law, while also praising the Cultural Revolution and “great democracy.” The Guangdong Provincial Party Committee organized hundreds of criticism meetings. Zhao Ziyang directed that the authors be allowed to answer back, and the criticism meetings often turned into debates. After 1976 it was escalated into a counterrevolutionary case, and the authors received rehabilitation in 1979. The questions it raised were the same ones Shanghai's worker rebels had run into and never answered.
1634: The Constitution passed by the Fourth National People's Congress in January 1975 included “speaking out freely, airing views fully, holding great debates, and writing big-character posters,” calling them a new form of socialist revolution created by the masses. The 1978 Constitution kept them. In 1980 the National People's Congress decided to remove them. On paper they were a right of the masses. During the Cultural Revolution they were used first of all to persecute people.
1637: Shadian, in Mengzi County, Yunnan, is a village of Hui Muslims. During the Cultural Revolution its mosque was shut and soldiers stationed there ate pork inside it. The Hui villagers petitioned many times to have their religious practice restored. In early July 1975 Wang Hongwen met representatives of the Shadian Hui and said, “If you still won't let the work team and the People's Liberation Army into the village, we will have to storm the mud fort.” From July 29 troops surrounded Shadian and nearby villages. By mid-August, by various counts, about 1,600 civilians had died, children among them, and most houses were destroyed. In 1979 the case was redressed and no longer labeled an “armed rebellion.” Some accounts hold that the order came from Deng Xiaoping, who was in charge of daily work. It was the largest military crackdown on civilians in the late Cultural Revolution, and many accounts skip over it.
1640: Purged early in the Cultural Revolution, he returned in 1973. From January 1975 he ran the daily work of the Party Central Committee, the State Council and the Military Affairs Commission, and pushed an across-the-board rectification. After the Tiananmen Incident in April 1976 he was again stripped of all posts. He returned in 1977 and later led reform and opening. For Wang Hongwen, he was the man who took power out of his hands in 1975. Wang Hongwen said, “What ‘in charge of daily work’? All the power is his now. The State Council is his, the army is his too. All I can do is run the central reading class.”

You lived at Diaoyutai. The houses were big and the corridors long. When you walked down them at night your footsteps carried all the way to the end. In the grounds there was a lake, with pine trees by the water, and wild hares.

It was called study, but no one set you any classes. Every day you read documents until late at night. You did not understand most of what was in them. What is foreign exchange, what is an import quota for fertilizer. You looked it all up word by word. ⟦0⟧

One day the Chairman, talking with you, mentioned an old text and told you to read it. In his Hunan accent you did not catch the title. You heard only a “Liu” and something ending in “zi.” You did not dare ask twice.

Some time later you went back to Shanghai and found Zhu Yongjia of the writing group. You asked if there was a text called Liu Something-zi. Zhu Yongjia thought for a moment and said it was the “Biography of Liu Penzi” in the “Book of the Later Han.” He found the book and explained it to you.

He spoke very slowly, as if to a student. Liu Penzi was a cowherd boy in the Red Eyebrows army, fifteen years old. Because he descended from the Han imperial house, he was picked by drawing lots and made emperor. He wore the emperor's robes and still often ran off to play with his cowherd friends. When the Red Eyebrows were defeated he surrendered to Liu Xiu. Liu Xiu did not kill him. He gave him some land to manage, and Liu Penzi lived to old age.

When Zhu Yongjia finished, he closed the book and looked at you. He did not say what the Chairman meant.

History In September 1972 Wang Hongwen was transferred to Beijing and lived at Diaoyutai. In 1973 Mao Zedong had him read the “Book of the Later Han: Biography of Liu Penzi,” with Zhu Yongjia explaining it. See Wikipedia, “Zhu Yongjia,” and the oral account by Zhu Yongjia and the introduction by Jin Guangyao listed in the handover notes (original texts pending). Diaoyutai had a lake, and Wang Hongwen often hunted and fished there, according to the recollections of Chen Shouxin, former deputy director of the Political Department of the Central Guard Regiment (cited in Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen”).

History Li Xun, “The Era of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), ch. 35, records that before the preparations for the Tenth Party Congress, Mao Zedong told Wang Hongwen to read the “Biography of Liu Penzi.” Wang did not catch the title and did not dare ask. Back in Shanghai he asked Zhu Yongjia for “Liu Something-zi,” and Zhu Yongjia guessed it was Liu Penzi (paraphrased). The same chapter records that at the Ninth Party Congress Wang Hongwen borrowed 15 yuan from Xu Jingxian to buy a pair of black Dacron trousers to wear for his speech.

Disputed There is still no reliable account of why Mao Zedong had him read the “Biography of Liu Penzi.” Zhu Yongjia's understanding at the time was that Mao hoped he would not be like Liu Penzi, someone nobody could prop up.

Fiction The scene of Zhu Yongjia's explanation and Wang Hongwen's reactions are the game's invention.

History From September 12, 1973, to May 29, 1974, Mao Zedong had Wang Hongwen accompany him 16 times when meeting foreign heads of state and government. On June 1, 1974, Zhou Enlai was hospitalized. On July 17 Mao Zedong criticized Jiang Qing, Wang Hongwen, Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan at a Politburo meeting as a “little faction of four.” See Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen” and “Fengqing Incident.”

Disputed On the private relationship between Jiang Qing and Wang Hongwen, Ross Terrill quotes a foreign Communist Party leader as saying Jiang Qing “poked him affectionately in the ribs” at a banquet. There is no solid evidence of anything more. The “kick under the table” is the game's invention.
1678: That day Jiang Qing kept you for dinner. You talked for three hours, all about the Premier and Deng Xiaoping. She said, the Chairman is old, and everyone around him is lying to him.
1679: That day Zhang Chunqiao talked with you for an hour. Most of the time you were the one talking. He said only one thing. Listen to the Chairman's words, and understand the Chairman's meaning.
1680: That day you went to the hospital. The Premier was very thin and wore hospital pajamas. He talked with you for an hour, about preparations for the Fourth National People's Congress and about getting along well with Comrade Xiaoping. He saw you to the door and stood there a long time, holding on to the door frame.
1681:
⟦0⟧

At the Politburo meeting on October 17, Jiang Qing brought out the materials on the Fengqing and pressed Deng Xiaoping to take a position. She asked whether he supported it or opposed it, or meant to stand in the middle. Deng Xiaoping said he had already read and circled the document and it still needed investigating, and that when the Politburo met to discuss things it should be on an equal footing. No one should treat people with that attitude. Jiang Qing kept on. Deng Xiaoping stood up and walked out.

⟦1⟧

That evening Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and you conferred in Building 17 at Diaoyutai. They said someone had to go to Changsha and report to the Chairman in person, ahead of everyone else. They all looked at you.

Early on the 18th, a plane for Changsha was waiting at Xijiao Airport. Once you got there, the Chairman would listen to you with his eyes half closed.
1682: At the meeting Jiang Qing also said that some comrades had sent over a thousand workers to Japan and America, and this too was a slavish worship of foreign things. She did not look at you. Everyone at the table glanced at you.
1683: “Beijing now has a strong smell of the Lushan Conference.”
1684: October 1974　Went to Changsha to report on work to Chairman Mao.
1685: October 18, 1974　Went to Changsha behind the Politburo's back to slander Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping.
1686: “If Deng Xiaoping keeps on like this, he'll be a second Lin Biao.”
1687: October 18, 1974　Went to Changsha behind the Politburo's back to slander Deng Xiaoping as a Lin Biao type.
1688: “On the Fengqing, Shanghai and the Ministry of Communications each have a point. I've come to hear the Chairman's view.”
1690: You did not go to Changsha. You phoned Jiang Qing and said objections should be raised face to face in the Politburo.
1691: October 1974　Insisted on discussing issues face to face within the Politburo.
1692: October 1974　Took an ambiguous stand in the Fengqing Incident.
1693:
History At the Politburo meeting on October 17, 1974, Jiang Qing used the Fengqing Incident to press Deng Xiaoping to take a position. Deng Xiaoping said, “When the Politburo meets to discuss things, it should be on an equal footing,” and walked out. That evening Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen conferred at Diaoyutai. On the 18th, without telling the other Politburo members, Wang Hongwen flew to Changsha and, in Building 6 of Guesthouse No. 9, told Mao Zedong that “Beijing now has a strong smell of the Lushan Conference.” See CPC News, “Chronicle of the Communist Party of China, 1974,” and Wikipedia, “Fengqing Incident.”

FictionThe fourth option appears only for players who visited Zhou Enlai in the hospital. It is the seed of the “working with Deng Xiaoping” dream.
1696:
The Chairman opened his eyes and looked at you for a long time. He said, go back.

You returned to Beijing. In November the Politburo met. You still had your seat, but no one brought documents to you first anymore. In December you and Premier Zhou went to Changsha together to report on preparations for the Fourth National People's Congress. The Chairman talked only with the Premier.

In January 1975 Deng Xiaoping became Vice Chairman, first Vice Premier, and Chief of the General Staff. In February a notice came from the center telling you to return to Shanghai to help with the work there.

In Shanghai you lived on Xingguo Road and went back to No. 17 Mill one day a week to work. People at the mill still called you Director Wang when they saw you, very quietly. In 1976 you learned what happened in Beijing from the newspapers. After October, people came to Xingguo Road and took you away. The man interrogating you said you were the first of the Gang of Four the Chairman had driven out of Beijing.
1697:
History went on as before. In 1975 Deng Xiaoping ran the daily work, and in April 1976 he was brought down again. In September the Chairman died.

On the evening of October 6, three people were arrested at Huairen Hall. The fourth was on Xingguo Road in Shanghai and was taken away the next morning. You did not attend the meetings of that week in Shanghai. By then you were no longer on the list. But the indictment still named you, calling you a member of the “Gang of Four” who ran a factional network in Shanghai.

In 1981 you were still sentenced to life. In court someone asked what you had said in Changsha in October 1974. You said, I said he was Lin Biao. Someone in the gallery drew a sharp breath.
1698: Charge　On October 18, 1974, went to Changsha and slandered Deng Xiaoping as a Lin Biao type.
1699: Disposition　From 1975, removed from the center and sent back to Shanghai.
1700: As written in 1977　Long a follower of Jiang Qing, framed Comrade Deng Xiaoping, and was sharply criticized by Chairman Mao.
1701: Afterward　The Vice Chairman elected at the Tenth Party Congress appeared from then on only on lists.
1702:
FictionIn history Wang Hongwen did go back to Shanghai in 1975, but he was not driven back. He was still Vice Chairman, and in 1976 he returned to Beijing.

History In December 1974 Mao Zedong told Wang Hongwen, “Don't form a Gang of Four” and “Don't form factions. Those who form factions will fall,” and from then on kept him at a distance. See Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen.”
1705: Jiang Qing cursed you once over the phone and hung up. Zhang Chunqiao later told you that after this, things would be hard for you with her. Deng Xiaoping ran into you in a corridor, nodded once, and said nothing.
1706: When the Chairman had heard you out, he said, if you have objections, raise them face to face. Doing it this way is no good. You must get along well with Comrade Xiaoping. When you go back, talk more with the Premier and Comrade Jianying. Don't gang up with Jiang Qing. Watch out for her. You flew back to Beijing that same day. In December the Chairman told you again, don't form a Gang of Four. Those who form factions will fall.
1707:
⟦0⟧

In November, Guangdong sent up some materials. A big-character poster had gone up on Beijing Road in Guangzhou, more than 26,000 characters on 67 sheets of newsprint, signed Li Yizhe and titled “On Socialist Democracy and the Legal System.”

You read it all the way through. It attacked Lin Biao and everything Lin Biao stood for. It also praised the Cultural Revolution and great democracy, and it praised you. It said that when the masses were persecuted, no law protected them. It said there had to be a legal system and democracy, that the democratic rights of the people had to be protected, and that privilege had to be limited.

You thought of the summer of 1966, when the work team put black materials into dossiers. You thought of Kangping Road, and of Kunshan.

Attached at the end was a request from the Guangdong Provincial Party Committee asking how the poster should be classified. The Fourth National People's Congress would open in January, and the new Constitution was to include speaking out freely, airing views fully, holding great debates, and writing big-character posters.
1708: Instruction: reactionary big-character poster, organize criticism.
1709: November 1974　Instructed that the reactionary big-character poster be criticized.
1710: November 1974　Instructed that it be criticized.
1711: Instruction: it may be criticized, the author may answer back, and no one may be beaten.
1712: November 1974　Instructed that a debate be held and the authors be allowed to answer back.
1713: November 1974　Took an ambiguous stand on the reactionary “Li Yizhe” poster.
1714: After the article on the “Four Bigs” in the draft Constitution, add one sentence. No one who puts up a big-character poster may be retaliated against for it.
1715: January 1975　Proposed that the Constitution guarantee the masses' right to put up big-character posters.
1716: January 1975　Backed reactionaries of the “Li Yizhe” type.
1717: Put the materials down. Go to the State Council and tell Deng Xiaoping you want to take charge of industry.
1718: 1975　Assisted Comrade Deng Xiaoping with rectification.
1720:
History In November 1974 a big-character poster signed “Li Yizhe” appeared in Guangzhou, titled “On Socialist Democracy and the Legal System.” It ran to more than 26,000 characters on 67 sheets of newsprint. Under the banner of criticizing the “Lin Biao system,” it called for democracy and rule of law, and also praised the Cultural Revolution, great democracy, and even Jiang Qing and Wang Hongwen. The Guangdong Provincial Party Committee organized hundreds of criticism meetings, and Zhao Ziyang directed that the authors be allowed to answer back. The Constitution passed by the Fourth National People's Congress in January 1975 included the “Four Bigs.” See Wikipedia, “Li Yizhe Incident.”

History For Mao Zedong's own words criticizing Wang Hongwen in Changsha, see Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen.”

Fiction The Li Yizhe materials reaching Wang Hongwen and his instructions on them are a game invention. The third option appears only for players who cited the Constitution, held to freedom of association, or held to 64 yuan in earlier acts. It is the seed of the “Four Bigs in the Constitution” dream.
1723:
From January on, Deng Xiaoping ran the daily work of the center. The State Council was his, the army was his too. What you ran was the central reading class. You told Xu Jingxian, all this was decided by the Chairman.

In early July a group of Hui representatives came from Yunnan, from Shadian. Their mosque had been shut early in the Cultural Revolution. A propaganda team had lived in the mosque, eaten pork in it, and thrown the bones into the well. They had petitioned for years to have the mosque opened. The province said they were making trouble. Troops were already outside the village.

You chaired the meeting. Among the representatives was an old man in a white cap who needed the young man beside him to interpret. He said, we are not against the Communist Party. We only want to be able to pray.

On the table lay talking points the province had written. One line said, if you still won't let the work team and the People's Liberation Army into the village, we will have to storm the mud fort.
1724: Read from the talking points. Say the last line looking at the old man.
1725: July 1975　Met Shadian Hui representatives and did ideological work with them.
1726: July 1975　Threatened and intimidated Shadian Hui representatives, with grave consequences.
1727: Turn the talking points face down. “About the mosques, one can open first. The troops stay out of the village for now. I'll talk to the Military Affairs Commission.”
1728: July 1975　Met Shadian Hui representatives and proposed measures to ease tensions.
1730: You did not speak. You had your secretary read the talking points. You wrote the old man's name in your notebook.
1731: July 1975　Met Shadian Hui representatives and made threats.
1732:
History In early July 1975 Wang Hongwen met representatives of the Shadian Hui and said, “We still have hopes for you. If you have made mistakes or committed crimes, atone for them through practical work... If you still won't let the work team and the People's Liberation Army into the village, we will have to storm the mud fort.” From July 29 troops surrounded Shadian and nearby villages. It ended in mid-August with heavy casualties. See Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen” and “Shadian Incident.” The propaganda team stationed in the mosque, eating pork there, and throwing pig bones into the well are from the same article.

Disputed Who gave the order. Wikipedia cites The Economist as saying Deng Xiaoping, then in charge of daily work, gave it. Other accounts stress that Wang Hongwen's speech was used as the basis. Wikipedia gives the death toll as about 1,600.

Fiction The old man in the white cap is the game's invention. The second and third options are game branches.
1735:
⟦0⟧

On July 29 the troops went into Shadian. A little over a week later a bulletin reached your desk. It said a counterrevolutionary armed rebellion had been put down. The bulletin had numbers. How many houses burned, how many guns seized, how many people dead. Among the dead were children.

⟦1⟧

That summer you hunted by the lake at Diaoyutai. At night you drove a jeep with the headlights on the grass, and the hares crouched in the light one by one and did not move. You fired many shots.
1736: You phoned the Military Affairs Commission. The voice on the line said, noted, we will look into it. Three days later the plan submitted by the Yunnan Provincial Party Committee was approved. Your name was not on the approval.
1737: When the secretary finished reading the talking points, the old man stood up, then sat down again.
1738: After you finished speaking, the old man said nothing more.
1739: You took out your notebook and looked for the old man's name. The bulletin had no names.
1740: The bulletin was thin. You finished reading it and signed “Read.”
1742: August 1975　Bore direct responsibility for the Shadian Incident.
1743:
History About 1,600 civilians died in the Shadian Incident, children among them, and most houses were destroyed. At the time it was labeled a “counterrevolutionary armed rebellion.” It was redressed in 1979. See Wikipedia, “Shadian Incident.” Wang Hongwen drove a jeep at night and hunted with powerful lights, according to the recollections of Chen Shouxin (cited in Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen”).

Fiction The look of the bulletin and Wang Hongwen's reactions are the game's invention. Whatever the player chooses, the outcome at Shadian does not change. This is the heaviest “inertia of history” in the game.
1746:
Premier Zhou died on the morning of January 8. The memorial meeting was in the Great Hall of the People. You stood in the second row. Deng Xiaoping read the eulogy and stopped for a long time halfway through.

Outside, Chang'an Avenue was full of people. When the hearse went by, no one had organized them. People stood along the road on their own, all the way from Xidan to Babaoshan. Some cried out loud.

⟦0⟧

In the car back to Diaoyutai, your secretary Liao Zukang asked whether you would go hunting that night. You said no.

At the end of January, word came that the man running the daily work of the center would be neither you nor Zhang Chunqiao. It would be Hua Guofeng.
1747: You remembered the summer of 1974 at the hospital, when he stood a long time holding on to the door frame.
1748: You remembered the day of the Tenth Party Congress, when he sat on the rostrum, right on your left.
